transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-07 14:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Dr. Eva Kline (CTO, Sparrow), Marcus Holt (Compliance), Rina Sato (Infra), Jonas Berg (ML Platform), Alyssa Ruiz (Procurement)

Summary: Short discovery — customer is regulated biotech with no internet on inference nodes; wants details for private/hermetic deployment, how offline updates work (signed manifests / USB media), hardware requirements and constraints, proof artifacts for audits, and rough timeline for running a bench.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir from Redwood. Quick intros, then we'll ask about your constraints, and Liam will walk through how we do hermetic updates and runtime constraints.
[00:18] Dr. Eva Kline: Hi all, Eva here. We're trying to replace an in-house inference piece with something we don't have to babysit. Our big no-no is any outbound connectivity from the lanes where models run.
[00:33] Marcus: From compliance side, we need deterministic audit logs, key custody proof, and an offline patch workflow that can be replayed in audits.
[00:45] Rina: Our datacenters are colos in EU, two candidate sites. Both have single top-of-rack switches with restricted egress, and that means no internet to GPU nodes.
[01:05] Samir: Got it. So sounds like Redwood Private hermetic option is in scope. Quick clarification — when you say no egress, is there any internal connectivity to a management VLAN, or fully isolated?
[01:20] Rina: Fully isolated compute VLAN for inference. There's a separate management plane in the same rack but it also has no external access; we can move files via sealed media and physical transfer.
[01:33] Liam: Good to know. That's our typical airgap scenario. We support update bundles that are signed with your on-prem HSM keys. You can verify signatures locally before loading. We call the agent that runs the verification the 'deployment verifier' — sometimes in notes it's transcribed as 'deployer-verif', so ignore that.
[01:55] Jonas: Walk me through manifest signing — do you expect us to generate keys externally or can Redwood help with ceremonies?
[02:10] Liam: We can provide a manifest template and a reference signing tool. For production you'll want keys inside your HSM (Luna or Thales), or an HSM appliance. The signing flow typically is: Redwood produces release bundle -> you validate and sign the manifest with your private key in the HSM -> transfer bundle into the hermetic environment -> local verifier checks signature and integrity and then applies.
[02:34] Marcus: That fits our audit model if logs are tamper-evident. Will Redwood store a copy of the signed manifest for tracing?
[02:45] Samir: We can optionally keep a copy in our control plane if you permit it, but for strict air-gap customers we usually avoid that. We support a ledger file that you can ingest into your internal audit systems.
[02:58] Dr. Eva Kline: What about rollback? If an update fails, we need guaranteed fallback and immutable snapshots.
[03:10] Liam: The runtime keeps a local image store and a KV cache snapshot. When a new bundle is applied we stage it, run validation hooks, then switch over. If healthchecks fail, it reverts to the last good image automatically. We also sign rollbacks so auditing shows chain of custody.
[03:34] [05:02] Samir: Switching to hardware: Rina, can you give an inventory preview? Jonas — any constraints on model sizes or throughput expectations?
[05:15] Rina: We have racks with either 2x A100 40GB (no NVLink) or single H100 80GB in some racks. Power per rack is limited to 12kW. Cooling is moderate — can't exceed 85% rack heat density. Also, no shared NVSwitch between hosts.
[05:36] Jonas: For model targets we're looking at a 13B LLM quantized to 4-bit for NLU tasks, and an 80–100 token window. Latency SLO is ~300ms p95. Throughput is modest, around 20-30 qps during peak.
[05:58] Liam: That helps. Without NVLink, multi-GPU sharded prompts have overhead; we typically recommend single-GPU placement for 13B 4-bit unless you do pipeline parallelism. Quantization can reduce memory but may affect quality tradeoffs; our Optimize team can run accuracy vs quantization tests.
[06:18] Dr. Eva: If we pick H100 in a single-socket config will we see meaningful latency improvements vs A100 for quantized workloads?
[06:30] Liam: H100 often wins on large context and FP16 kernels, but for heavily quantized 4-bit kernels difference is smaller. We'll bench both. We'll also check VRAM headroom for cache (KV cache requirements) because chat workloads can spike memory.
[06:48] [08:10] Marcus: On encryption and key custody: can Redwood integrate with our on-prem KMS? We must ensure the private keys never leave the HSM.
[08:25] Samir: Yes — typical pattern is keys stay in your HSM. Redwood provides tooling that signs the release manifest on your side; our agents only verify. We can also support enveloped key handling for model artifacts if you need encryption-at-rest on disk with keys derived from the HSM.
[08:45] Rina: Do you support hardware attestation? We want to prove host integrity to Compliance during audit.
[08:55] Liam: We have hooks for TPM-based attestation and can produce attestation statements from the node's boot measurements. For full attestation chain we'll coordinate with your infra to read quotes and embed them into the release record. It's additional engineering but we've done it with other regulated customers.
[09:20] [11:00] Jonas: About runtime upgrades — what's the expected downtime for a node during a patch?
[11:10] Liam: Patching typically takes 5–15 minutes per node to apply and validate depending on model sizes and cold start costs. If you want zero downtime we can do rolling patches across a pool with load balancing. In hermetic setups you'll likely stage an update on an idle node, run checks, then switch traffic.
[11:31] Dr. Eva: Are there minimum OS/hypervisor constraints? We run RHEL 8 with minimal kernel hardening and containerd but no external registries.
[11:44] Liam: We support baremetal containers or systemd-managed runtime. For hermetic installs we supply tarball bundles and a small bootstrap image; you can install offline. For RHEL8 it's supported, we just require kernel modules for our kernel-accelerated ops (we supply signed modules).
[12:02] [13:50] Marcus: We need traceability for every inference: which model, version, which manifest, who signed it and that signature timestamp. Can Redwood provide that in a per-request trace?
[13:05] Samir: We emit token-level metadata and per-request headers with model/version/manifest SHA. In hermetic mode the local log contains the same fields; we can provide log schemas and an example loader for your SIEM. Logs are append-only and can be exported as signed bundles.
[13:29] Jonas: Any concerns about clock drift affecting signed timestamps? We don't have NTP to external time sources in air-gapped.
[13:40] Liam: We handle that by relying on your internal time authority — as long as your management VLAN has a secure internal time source, we record local time and include the signing timestamp from the manifest. For audits, cross-validate the HSM time. We can accept signed timestamp counters from an HSM as authoritative.
[14:05] [16:00] Alyssa: Procurement question — what's the typical procurement structure for Private hermetic? Capex plus annual support? Is there a minimum term?
[16:12] Samir: Usually it's a license+deployment fee and then annual support. For hermetic customers there's an onboarding fee for the offline tooling and manifest workflows. Terms are flexible; we'll draft a 12-month baseline with options for dedicated reserved capacity.
[16:31] Alyssa: Lead times for hardware? We might need Redwood to support more models later—do you provide a hardware compatibility matrix?
[16:42] Liam: We'll send a compatibility matrix. For specific GPUs we show bandwidth/perf expectations, and typical rack power profiles. We'll also note recommended drivers and exact kernel module versions.
[16:58] [19:00] Rina: One operational constraint — we do maintenance windows monthly for the whole cluster; we rarely have spare capacity. Is there a plan for blue-green in hermetic setups?
[19:12] Liam: Yes, but it requires a second set of nodes or capacity reservations. For very constrained sites we recommend a small warm spare pool (1–2 nodes) to handle updates without impacting traffic. We'll help size that based on bench results.
[19:40] Dr. Eva: What about model provenance? We need to show where the base model came from and any quantization steps.
[19:52] Samir: We maintain model provenance metadata — source commit, tokenizer versions, quantization recipe. We'll include the provenance in the signed manifest so auditors can trace back every artifact.
[20:10] [22:00] Marcus: For audits, we need sample artifacts: signed manifests, logs, attestation statements, and a runbook. Can Redwood provide a package that simulates an audit trace?
[22:16] Liam: Yes — we can provide an 'audit bundle' example that includes a release manifest, signature chain, node attestation quotes, and log snippets. We'll include that in the docs pack.
[22:32] Jonas: About benchmarking — do you want sample workload or will Redwood provide synthetic?
[22:40] Samir: We'll take a small sample dataset from you (anonymized) and run a replica bench plus a synthetic latency profile for edge cases. We'll need a test node image to be installed in your isolated lab or we can bring a cloud-backed test harness mirrored to a hermetic environment.
[22:58] Rina: Cloud mirror is harder; we'd prefer to run the bench in our lab with zero egress.
[23:08] Liam: That's fine. We'll provide a tiny tarball with the bench runner and a signed manifest; you can run it and return the results. We'll also do a remote pair-programmed session while you run it (over a VPN to the management plane) if allowed.
[23:32] [26:00] Alyssa: Licensing questions — do you do per-token billing for private or a flat seat/license?
[26:10] Samir: For Private we usually do a capacity-based subscription (nodes or vGPU equivalent) plus a support SLA. We can overlay usage metrics and provide an optional per-token reconciliation for chargeback inside your org.
[26:28] Jonas: If we want to change model versions frequently, what's the oper cost?
[26:36] Liam: It's an operational step: create signed bundle, transfer, stage, and flip. With automation it can be minutes, but for strict audit you'll likely keep a cadence (weekly or monthly) and follow review steps. The Optimize team helps reduce churn by using dynamic routing to cheaper variants if you need frequent small changes.
[26:58] [29:00] Marcus: Any third-party dependencies we should list for procurement — e.g., HSM vendor, driver support, special NV drivers?
[29:12] Samir: We'll send a short procurement checklist: supported HSM vendors (Thales, Luna, AWS CloudHSM if you have a connected mgmt plane), GPU drivers, kernel modules, and a note about licensing on certain accelerator features.
[29:34] Rina: A practical question — can we seed models via signed USB drives? Our process is manual: ship USB, scan on an offline scanner, then a human performs import.
[29:46] Liam: Yes, USB or physical media is common. We recommend checksums and signature verification scripts in the toolchain. Also include an airgap chain-of-custody log documenting who touched media and when.
[30:02] [32:00] Dr. Eva: Security — do you support role-based access and SSO for management plane that is separate from runtime? Our compliance requires RBAC and SAML SSO for any control actions.
[32:12] Samir: The control plane (if you opt in) supports SAML/SSO and RBAC. For hermetic customers many choose a customer-managed control plane behind SSO. Runtime-level RBAC maps to management plane identities and local service accounts. We'll detail the mapping in docs.
[32:34] Jonas: Is there a small demo or proof artifact we can show to governance team next week?
[32:42] Samir: We can produce a short 'attestation + signed-manifest' demo and an audit bundle; Liam will prepare it.
[32:52] Liam: I'll prepare a 10-slide tech appendix and the signed-manifest sample.
[33:06] [36:00] Marcus: One red flag we watch: any cloud callbacks. Can you guarantee no telemetry leaves the hermetic network unless explicitly packaged and approved?
[36:16] Samir: We guarantee no automatic outbound telemetry. Any artifact exported is a customer-initiated signed bundle. We can also provide local-only debug artifacts that never leave nodes.
[36:30] Rina: If we want to do remote debugging in a crisis, what's the process?
[36:40] Samir: We offer an emergency remote assistance workflow: you provision a short-lived secure tunnel from the management VLAN to Redwood SE during the session, and we require explicit signed consent and an engineer present physically. All session transcripts are logged as part of the audit bundle.
[36:58] [39:00] Jonas: Regarding model updates and quantization — if we request custom quantization recipes, can Redwood run those in your optimize lab?
[39:10] Liam: Yes, our Optimize team will run quantization experiments and provide delta reports on accuracy and latency. For hermetic setups we can ship quantized artifacts with provenance.
[39:26] Dr. Eva: Rough timeline — if we greenlight a small bench this month, when could we have a pilot?
[39:38] Samir: Bench next week, two weeks for validation, then pilot could start 4–6 weeks afterwards depending on procurement. Given your audit schedules, Marcus, how does that fit?
[39:52] Marcus: That should work if we have audit artifacts within 3 weeks.
[40:03] [42:00] Alyssa: Anything else you need from Procurement now?
[42:12] Samir: The PO cadence and a point of contact are enough for now. We'll send an MSA template for review.
[42:22] Alyssa: Great.
[42:28] [44:00] Liam: Quick recap of technical asks from our side: hardware inventory, power/cooling, kernel/OS versions, HSM vendor and whether you can run a time authority on the mgmt plane. We'll package the bench runner and signed-manifest example.
[44:46] Rina: We'll compile that.
[45:00] Samir: Recap for next steps: we'll send hermetic checklist, docs, SOC2 artifacts, sample signed manifest, and bench runner. Customer to share HW inventory and procurement constraints. We'll schedule the bench the week of 2027-04-19.
[45:22] Dr. Eva: Thanks — that matches our expectations. We'll aim to have Rina and Marcus drive the artifact collection.
[45:32] [47:00] Jonas: One last quick question — what logging retention do you recommend for audit?
[47:10] Samir: Typically 12 months for high-sensitivity labs, but you'll want at least 90 days hot and 12 months cold. We can provide compression and signed archival bundles.
[47:26] Marcus: We'll likely go 2 years for certain artifacts, but that is internal policy.
[47:36] [50:00] Samir: Alright — we'll follow up by email with the checklist and propose bench dates. Thanks everyone.
[50:12] Meeting adjourned.
